---
title: "Grades based on standardised evidence"
subtitle: "3.3 · a constructed comparator after the postrank theory book, ch. 2 and 17"
description: "Directional statements induced by flags constructed from estimates and standard errors."
---

A standardised-evidence rule compares an estimate with a reference using
$z_i = (\widehat\theta_i-r)/SE_i$. Here the reference r is zero. Values above the upper cutoff receive the highest
flag, values below the lower cutoff receive the lowest, and the remainder receive the middle flag. Interpreting
these flags as ordered grades can place a smaller estimate above a larger one, since the classification also
depends on sampling precision. The example evaluates the resulting pairwise statement under alternative normal
posterior specifications while keeping the flag rule explicit.


## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Two units, flat prior.** A has z = 4.00 and B has z = 1.50. The flags state A above B, although B's estimate
  is larger. Taking each true value as normal around its estimate, with its SE, gives error probability .686 and
  risk .6862. The estimate bars and standardised positions display the source of the reversed order.
- **Same flags, teaching prior.** The error falls to .288; the posterior means are .180 for A and .108 for B.
  The flags stay put: they use estimates and SEs, while the selected posterior prices their stated direction.
- **B’s SE .15.** B reaches z = 2.00. Both units now receive the same flag, so the report states 0 pairs and has
  risk .2000. A shared grade withholds a direction; it does not assert that the true values are equal.
- **Cutoff 2.576.** The stricter cutoff separates the flags again. The stated direction has error .736. Changing an estimate or SE can change its flag; changing τ affects only the withholding cost.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="In practice"}
The rule flags a unit above or below the reference when $|z_i|$ is more than 1.96, that is, when its difference
from the reference is statistically significant at the .05 level.

This constructed comparator follows the postrank theory book, ch. 17 (the Tennessee
procedure in ch. 2 uses a related index with other cutoffs).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="In postrank"}
```r
p <- pnorm((.30-.20)/sqrt(.05^2+.20^2))
x <- postrank::postrank_probabilities(array(c(NA,1-p,p,NA),c(2,2,1),dimnames=list(c("A","B"),c("A","B"),"score")), event="directional_error", zero_ties=TRUE, margin=0, source=list(kind="analytic_reference",description="Two-unit example",conditioning="Independent flat-prior normals"), targets=c(score="True value; larger is higher priority"))
postrank::postrank_evaluate(c(A=1L,B=2L),x,weights=c(score=1),tau=.2)[c("N","E_over_N","primary_risk")]
```
:::

Standalone: [evidence-flags](../../embed/evidence-flags.html), for example `?seB=.15&crit=2.576`.

Related applications: [Standardised-evidence flags in a league](flags-in-the-league.qmd), [The decision for an isolated pair](../grades/one-pair.qmd).
